pos: n. (John Cameron, c. 1579–1625, Scottish theologian, professor at Saumur, Sedan and Glasgow, teacher of Amyraut)
etymology: Scottish Gaelic cam sròn, crooked nose; John, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: John Cameron was a Glasgow prodigy who read Greek publicly at twenty, went to France, and spent most of his life teaching in the Huguenot academies of Bordeaux, Sedan and Saumur. His learning was prodigious and his judgement less so. He taught that the will is moved not by a physical operation of grace but by a moral suasion in which the illumined understanding draws the will infallibly after it, and he distinguished the divine decrees in a way his pupil Amyraut would develop into the hypothetical-universalist scheme. Brought back to Glasgow as Principal in 1622, he defended the royal supremacy in church matters, was driven out within a year, and died at Montauban after being assaulted in the street for the same opinions. The dictionary honours his labours in the biblical languages and rejects his account of grace. John 6:44 will not be reduced to persuasion: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.” Eze 37:9 shows the kind of work required, breath commanded into slain men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines suasion as the act of persuading; and regeneration, in theology, as the change of heart by which men are prepared for heaven; the renovation of the heart by the Spirit.
webster_full: SUA'SION, n. The act of persuading; persuasion.

REGENERA'TION, n. In theology, new birth by the grace of God; that change by which the will and natural enmity of man to God and his law are subdued, and a principle of supreme love to God is implanted in the heart.
ILLUMINA'TION, n. The act of supplying with light; infusion of intellectual light, knowledge or grace.
scriptures: John 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Eze 37:9
Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live.
Tit 3:5
Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;
John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Moral suasion is too small a word for what Scripture describes when a dead man is made to live.
corruption_paragraphs: Cameron's scheme makes the Spirit's work an enlightening of the mind so persuasive that the will cannot but follow. It is not Pelagian and it is not quite Reformed. The objection is that Scripture describes regeneration with the vocabulary of creation and resurrection, not of argument. Tit 3:5 calls it a washing and a renewing; John 3:3 calls it a birth; Eze 37:9 pictures it as breath entering the slain. None of those is a persuasion, and a corpse is not undecided.

The modern descendant of the error is the evangelistic method that treats conversion as the outcome of sufficiently compelling presentation, so that a failure to convert becomes a failure of technique. John 6:44 forecloses it. The drawing is the Father's, it is indispensable, and it is effectual. Preachers are to reason, plead and persuade with all their strength, and then to know that the life comes from elsewhere.
roots_summary: Greek helkuo (G1670), to draw; palingenesia (G3824), regeneration; Hebrew ruach (H7307), breath, spirit.
roots_lines: Greek helkuo (G1670) — to draw, to drag; John 6:44.
Greek gennao (G1080) — to beget, to be born; John 3:3.
usage: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44) — drawing, not merely urging.
“by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost” (Tit 3:5) — the vocabulary of new creation.
“breathe upon these slain, that they may live” (Eze 37:9) — what preaching cannot do by itself.

pos: n. pl. (the Articles of Religion of the Church of Ireland, adopted 1615, drafted chiefly by James Ussher)
etymology: From Ireland; article, from Latin articulus, a joint, a small part.
biblical_def: The Irish Articles of 1615 were the confession of the Church of Ireland, drafted largely by James Ussher and adopted by the Dublin convocation. In one hundred and four articles they go well beyond the Thirty-Nine Articles of England in their Reformed precision: they teach absolute predestination and reprobation in plain terms, name the pope as antichrist, set out a careful doctrine of the covenants and of the Sabbath, and enumerate the canonical books while excluding the apocryphal. They are the chief bridge between the Elizabethan settlement and the Westminster Confession of 1646, which borrows their structure and in places their wording. Ussher himself attended no Westminster session, but his articles sat on the desk. Jude 1:3 is the principle of such documents, that the faith was “once delivered unto the saints” and must be confessed as received. 2Ti 1:13 supplies the form: “Hold fast the form of sound words.” A confession is not a second Bible but a public answer to the question of what this church believes the Bible to teach.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an article, in a religious sense, as a point of faith; a distinct proposition in a connected series of such propositions; and a confession of faith, as a public avowal of belief.
webster_full: 'ARTICLE, n. A single clause in a contract, account, system of regulations, treaty, or other writing; a particular.
'ARTICLE, n. A point of faith; a distinct proposition in a connected series of such propositions; as the thirty nine articles.
CONFES'SION, n. Avowal; the acknowledgment of a crime, fault, or something to one's disadvantage. Profession; avowal of a religious faith.
scriptures: Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
corruption_summary: Ireland confessed in 1615 what England would not put in writing until Westminster, and Westminster read Ireland's draft.
corruption_paragraphs: Confessions are charged in our day with freezing a living faith into dead propositions. The charge misunderstands what a confession is for. 1Ti 3:15 calls the church the pillar and ground of the truth, and a pillar is a public, immovable, load-bearing thing. A church that will not say in writing what it believes has not escaped having a doctrine; it has only made its doctrine unaccountable, which is the condition every heresy prefers.

The other misuse is to set the confession above the text it confesses. Isa 8:20 sends every claim back to the law and to the testimony, and the Irish Articles themselves do this, grounding each proposition in cited Scripture. The Reformed position is subordinate standards: binding on officers, revisable by the church, always answerable to the word. A confession is a fence around a field, not the field.
roots_summary: Greek pistis (G4102), faith; hupotuposis (G5296), form, pattern; Hebrew torah (H8451), law.
roots_lines: Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, the body of what is believed; Jude 1:3.
Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — an outline, a pattern; 2 Timothy 1:13.
Greek hedraioma (G1477) — a stay, a support, ground; 1 Timothy 3:15.
usage: “the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3) — what a confession confesses.
“Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13) — the warrant for written standards.
“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — what every article answers to.

pos: n. (Robert Baillie, 1602–1662, Scottish minister, commissioner to the Westminster Assembly, Principal of Glasgow University, diarist)
etymology: Scottish Baillie, a magistrate, from Old French bailli; Robert, Germanic, bright fame.
biblical_def: Robert Baillie is the eyewitness. One of the Scottish commissioners sent to the Westminster Assembly in 1643, he wrote letters and kept journals that remain the fullest surviving account of what was said in that room, day by day, for four years. He was a moderate Presbyterian who disliked both the Independents' polity and the king's execution, served as Principal of Glasgow from 1661, and died the next year as the Restoration began dismantling the settlement he had helped build. His testimony matters because he was not a partisan chronicler: he records the Scots' frustrations, the Independents' skill in debate, and his own misgivings with equal candour. Act 4:20 describes the instinct that produced the Letters and Journals: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.” Heb 13:7 commands the use later generations are to make of such records, to remember them which have the rule and, “considering the end of their conversation,” to follow their faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a journal as a diary; an account of daily transactions and events; and a commissioner, as a person who has a commission or warrant to perform some office.
webster_full: JOUR'NAL, n. A diary; an account of daily transactions and events; or the book containing such account.
COMMIS'SIONER, n. A person who has a commission or warrant to perform some office, or execute some business, for the person or government which employs him.
CHRON'ICLE, n. An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
scriptures: Act 4:20
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
corruption_summary: The Westminster Assembly is known to us in its daily detail because one Scotsman could not stop writing letters home.
corruption_paragraphs: Baillie's candour is the point worth pressing. He did not flatter his own party, and the Assembly is more credible to posterity because its friendliest chronicler recorded its quarrels. Act 20:27 sets the standard for a minister, not to shun declaring the whole counsel of God, and the same refusal to edit applies to a church's account of itself. Histories written to protect a movement's reputation protect nothing; they merely transfer the reckoning to a generation that will find the suppressed documents.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of honest record. Psa 68:11 celebrates the great company of those that published the word, and publishing includes the plain minutes of what the church actually did. A denomination that keeps no honest archive has decided in advance that its grandchildren should not be able to examine it.
roots_summary: Greek laleo (G2980), to speak; anastrophe (G391), conversation, manner of life; boule (G1012), counsel.
roots_lines: Greek laleo (G2980) — to speak, to utter; Acts 4:20.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to lead, to have the rule over; Hebrews 13:7.
Greek anastrophe (G391) — manner of life, conversation; Hebrews 13:7.
Hebrew basar (H1319) — to publish, to bear tidings; Psalm 68:11.
usage: “we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20) — the diarist's compulsion.
“Remember them which have the rule over you” (Heb 13:7) — why the record is kept.
“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — the whole of it, unedited.

pos: n. pl. (the followers of Richard Cameron; the strictest Covenanting societies of the Killing Time, afterwards the Reformed Presbyterians)
etymology: From Cameron, the field preacher Richard Cameron; the suffix -ian, a follower of.
biblical_def: The Cameronians were the remnant of the Scottish Covenanters who, after the Sanquhar Declaration of 1680, disowned Charles Stuart as a covenant-breaker and refused every indulgence the crown offered. They met in field conventicles under armed guard, were hunted across the southwest moors through the Killing Time, and organized themselves into praying societies with no ministers at all after Renwick's execution in 1688. Their claim was narrow and consistent: that Scotland had covenanted nationally with God, that the crown had broken the covenant, and that no man may obey a magistrate who commands what God forbids. In 1689 many enlisted in the regiment that still bore their name. Act 5:29 is the whole of their politics: “We ought to obey God rather than men.” Heb 11:38 is the whole of their history, of men of whom the world was not worthy, who “wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.” The dictionary honours their refusal and notes soberly where rigour hardened into separation from brethren who had conceded less.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as an assembly for religious worship; appropriately, an assembly of dissenters from the established church; and nonconformity, as neglect or failure of conformity.
webster_full: CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly or meeting; appropriately, an assembly of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship.
COV'ENANTER, n. One who makes a covenant. In Scottish history, one who subscribed the national covenant.
NONCONFORM'ITY, n. Neglect or failure of conformity; in England, the refusal to unite with an established church.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: The strictest of the Covenanters were right about the crown and sometimes wrong about their brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: Two judgements must be held at once. On the central matter the Cameronians were right, and the indulgences they refused were exactly what the crown designed them to be: a way of buying the Kirk's silence with a licence. Mat 10:28 is the calculation they made correctly, fearing him who can destroy both soul and body rather than the dragoons. Rev 12:11 names their weapons and their price, the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and lives not loved unto the death.

Where they erred was in treating every lesser compromise as apostasy and unchurching ministers who had accepted an indulgence under pressure. Rigour that cannot distinguish between a traitor and a frightened brother ends by having no brethren left. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that conscience bound by Scripture must not bend to the state, and that the same conscience owes patience to weaker men standing in the same fire.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; marturia (G3141), testimony; Hebrew midbar, desert places.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
Greek nikao (G3528) — to overcome, to conquer; Revelation 12:11.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the Sanquhar principle.
“they wandered in deserts, and in mountains” (Heb 11:38) — the moors of Galloway.
“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — the price they paid.

pos: n. (John Brown of Wamphray, c. 1610–1679, Scottish Covenanter minister, exile in Holland, controversialist against the indulgences)
etymology: English Brown, a colour-name surname; Wamphray, a parish in Dumfriesshire.
biblical_def: John Brown of Wamphray was minister of Wamphray in Annandale until the Restoration ejected him in 1662. Imprisoned in Edinburgh and then banished, he spent the rest of his life in the Netherlands, mostly at Rotterdam, writing the books the hunted societies at home could not write for themselves. His Apologetical Relation of 1665 defended the ejected ministers and the lawfulness of resisting a tyrannical magistrate, and was burnt by the hangman in Edinburgh. He wrote against the indulgences, against Episcopal church government, and at length on justification and on the Christian's life hid with Christ. He is not to be confused with John Brown of Haddington, the later Secession commentator. Psa 11:3 is the question his pamphlets answer: “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” Heb 13:7 is the use his exile serves, remembering those who spoke the word of God and following their faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country; and apology, as a defense; an excuse; something said or written in defense.
webster_full: EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country or place of residence by authority.
APOL'OGY, n. A defense; something said or written in defense or extenuation of what appears to others wrong.
EJEC'TION, n. The act of casting out; expulsion; the act of discharging from office.
scriptures: Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
Heb 13:7
Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of their conversation.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
corruption_summary: Banished to Rotterdam, he armed the field preachers at home with arguments they had no press to print.
corruption_paragraphs: Exile has been one of God's standing methods for distributing a persecuted church's literature. Act 8:4 is the pattern: the scattered “went every where preaching the word,” and the scattering was the persecution. Brown's Dutch years produced more for Scotland than his Annandale parish could have. A government that silences a man at home and lets him live abroad has usually multiplied him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lawfulness and duty of written defence. Brown did not take up arms; he took up a pen and argued from Scripture that the magistrate who commands sin forfeits obedience in that command, which is Act 5:29 applied. Churches under pressure today often reach first for public relations and only later, if ever, for a reasoned theological case. He reached for the case.
roots_summary: Hebrew shath (H8356), foundations; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad; euaggelizo (G2097), to preach good tidings.
roots_lines: Greek euaggelizo (G2097) — to announce good news; Acts 8:4.
usage: “If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3) — the Restoration in one line.
“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — exile as distribution.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the Apologetical Relation in brief.

pos: n. (the declaration posted at Sanquhar, Dumfriesshire, 22 June 1680, by Richard Cameron and twenty armed Covenanters, disowning Charles II)
etymology: Sanquhar, from Gaelic sean càthair, old fort; declaration, from Latin declarare, to make clear.
biblical_def: The Sanquhar Declaration was read aloud at the market cross of a small Dumfriesshire burgh by a band of twenty men who then nailed it to the cross and rode away. It disowned Charles Stuart as king, on the ground that he had broken the covenants he swore at his coronation, had usurped the crown rights of Christ over His church, and had made war on his own subjects for worshipping God. It declared war against him as a tyrant and against James, Duke of York, as a papist successor. One month later Cameron was killed at Airds Moss. Nothing in British history quite matches the arithmetic: twenty men against a kingdom, in writing, signed. Act 5:29 is its first premise. Act 4:12 is its second, that the sole headship of Christ is not transferable, and that no earthly supremacy may stand in that place. Mat 10:28 explains how twenty men do such a thing and then go home to supper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a declaration as an affirmation; a public announcement or proclamation; and a tyrant, as a despotic ruler; a cruel master; an oppressor.
webster_full: DECLARA'TION, n. An affirmation; a public announcement or proclamation of a fact or an intention.
TY'RANT, n. A monarch or other ruler or master, who uses power to oppress his subjects; a cruel master; an oppressor.
SUPREM'ACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
corruption_summary: Twenty men published a declaration of war against a king because he had claimed a headship that belongs to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The theological nerve of Sanquhar is the crown rights of Christ over His church. The Stuart supremacy was not merely oppressive; it asserted that the king determines the government, worship and discipline of the church of God. Act 4:12 says there is no other name under heaven given among men whereby we must be saved, and the exclusivity there is total. A magistrate who makes himself the church's head has stepped into the one place that is occupied.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. What presses now is softer and harder to see: the state claiming to define what a church may teach, whom it may employ, and which doctrines count as acceptable. The principle to recover is that the church's obedience to the magistrate is real but bounded, and that the boundary is not a matter of preference. Mat 10:28 supplies the courage; Act 5:29 supplies the rule.
roots_summary: Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; onoma (G3686), name; apokteino (G615), to kill.
roots_lines: Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; Acts 5:29.
usage: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — nailed to a market cross.
“there is none other name under heaven given among men” (Act 4:12) — the crown rights of Christ.
“fear not them which kill the body” (Mat 10:28) — how twenty men dared.

pos: n. (the battle at Bothwell Bridge on the Clyde, 22 June 1679, where the Covenanter army was broken by Monmouth's forces)
biblical_def: Bothwell Bridge was the end of the Covenanters as a field army. Three weeks after their victory at Drumclog, some four to six thousand gathered on the Clyde, and spent the interval quarrelling over whether to admit men who had accepted the king's indulgence and whether to petition or defy. The dispute was still unsettled when Monmouth's regulars forced the bridge. The rout was swift; perhaps four hundred were killed and twelve hundred taken prisoner, penned for months in Greyfriars kirkyard at Edinburgh, and many shipped for the plantations, of whom some two hundred drowned when their vessel struck the Orkney rocks. The lesson the Covenanters drew was bitter and correct: an army divided over the terms of its own confession cannot stand in the field. Ecc 4:9 states the plain principle, that “Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.” Psa 11:3 is what the survivors asked afterwards.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rout as the defeat and confusion of an army or band of troops; and division, as disunion; discord; variance; difference.
webster_full: ROUT, n. The defeat and confusion of an army or band of troops, or the disorder and confusion of troops thus defeated.
DIVIS'ION, n. Disunion; discord; variance; difference.
CAP'TIVE, n. A prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war, by an enemy.
scriptures: Ecc 4:9
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
Psa 11:3
If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: They lost the bridge arguing about the indulgence, which is a parable about parties that are right and divided.
corruption_paragraphs: The hard mercy in this history is that God did not reward a righteous cause held by a quarrelling people. Ecc 4:9 is not sentimental about unity; it is practical, promising a good reward for labour shared. The Covenanters at Bothwell had the better argument and the worse discipline, and discipline is what a bridge requires. Christian movements that cannot settle their secondary questions before the enemy arrives will settle them in the rout.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nor should the lesson be read as a counsel to paper over real doctrinal difference for the sake of effectiveness; the indulgence question was not trivial. The principle to recover is that the time to resolve a church's internal division is before the crisis, in councils and in patience, and that Heb 11:38 honours the scattered survivors as men of whom the world was not worthy whether or not they held the bridge.
roots_summary: Hebrew shenayim (H8147), two; sakar (H7939), reward; Greek planao (G4105), to wander.
usage: “Two are better than one” (Ecc 4:9) — the lesson of the bridge.
“If the foundations be destroyed, what can the righteous do?” (Psa 11:3) — asked in Greyfriars kirkyard.
“Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — the verdict above the verdict.

pos: n. (the skirmish at Drumclog in Lanarkshire, 1 June 1679, the one Covenanter victory in the field)
etymology: Scottish Gaelic druim, a ridge, with clog, a bell or rounded hill.
biblical_def: Drumclog was a conventicle that became a battle. On the first Sunday of June 1679 a field preaching on the moor near Loudoun Hill was interrupted by John Graham of Claverhouse and a troop of dragoons. The armed worshippers, perhaps two hundred and fifty with pikes and a few muskets, drew up behind a bog, let the cavalry founder in it, and routed them; Claverhouse escaped on a wounded horse. It is the only clear Covenanter victory of the Killing Time, and three weeks later it was cancelled at Bothwell Bridge. The event is remembered less for its military consequence than for what it reveals: that these were congregations, not armies, gathered to hear sermons with swords laid beside them because hearing sermons had been made a capital matter. Zec 4:6 is the right caution against making too much of the victory: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.” Heb 11:38 remains the better epitaph.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a conventicle as an assembly of dissenters from the established church for religious worship; and a skirmish, as a slight fight in war.
webster_full: SKIRM'ISH, n. A slight fight in war; a light combat between small parties, or a desultory contest.
CONVEN'TICLE, n. An assembly of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship.
MOOR, n. A tract of land overgrown with heath; a marsh; a fen; a tract of low watery ground.
scriptures: Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: A congregation with pikes beat a troop of dragoons on a Sunday, and then lost everything three weeks later.
corruption_paragraphs: Drumclog tempts its admirers into a theology of the sword, and the Covenanters' own best men resisted that. Zec 4:6 was written to a man rebuilding a temple with enemies around him, and it does not say the walls are unnecessary; it says the outcome is the Spirit's. One victory on a bog did not establish the covenanted kingdom, and the men who read it as a sign were disabused at Bothwell.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Drumclog actually demonstrates: that the right to gather for worship is not the state's to grant, and that a people who will carry weapons to a sermon have understood what is at stake better than a people who will not carry a Bible to work. Act 5:29 is why they were on the moor at all.
roots_lines: Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, an army, might; Zechariah 4:6.
usage: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” (Zec 4:6) — the caution over a victory.
“Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — the moor congregations.
“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — why the conventicle met at all.

pos: n. (the battle of Rullion Green in the Pentland Hills, 28 November 1666, ending the Pentland Rising)
etymology: Scots rullion, a rough shoe or a coarse person; green, a grassy place.
biblical_def: Rullion Green ended the first armed rising of the Covenanters after the Restoration. It began in Galloway when four countrymen intervened to stop soldiers torturing an old man over unpaid church fines; the scuffle grew into a march of some nine hundred, badly armed and soaked by November rain, which reached the Pentland Hills within sight of Edinburgh and found no city rising to meet it. Sir Thomas Dalyell's regulars caught them at Rullion Green in the dusk. About fifty were killed and eighty taken; the prisoners were tortured with the boot and hanged in batches, and their severed limbs were set up in towns across the southwest as a warning. The warning failed, and the Killing Time followed. Rev 2:10 is the promise over such a scene: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.” Mat 10:28 is the arithmetic the hangings could not alter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rising as an insurrection; a revolt; and a martyr, as one who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith.
webster_full: RI'SING, n. The act of rising; insurrection; a tumultuous assembly.
M'ARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith, or by reason of his adherence to it.
GIB'BET, n. A gallows; a post with an arm projecting, on which criminals were formerly hanged in chains.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

corruption_summary: A rising begun by four men defending a neighbour ended with heads on spikes across Galloway, and recruited a generation.
corruption_paragraphs: The state's calculation at Rullion Green was that displayed cruelty deters. It is a calculation that has been made against the church in every century and has a consistent record. Rev 12:11 explains why it fails, for the overcoming is by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony by men who loved not their lives unto the death; a threat has no purchase on a man who has already surrendered the thing threatened.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Rev 2:10's ordering of fear and reward: the tribulation is named, limited and permitted, and the crown is promised on the far side of death and not before it. Martyr histories go wrong when they promise deliverance in this life. Scripture promises a crown of life, and the Pentland prisoners received it on the scaffold.

“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — why the terror failed.
“fear not them which kill the body” (Mat 10:28) — the arithmetic of the boot.

pos: n. pl. (Margaret Wilson and Margaret McLachlan, drowned in the Solway tide at Wigtown, Galloway, 11 May 1685)
etymology: Wigtown, Old English wic, a dwelling, with tūn, an enclosure; martyr, from Greek martus, a witness.
biblical_def: The Wigtown Martyrs were two women, one of about eighteen and one of about sixty-three, condemned for refusing the oath abjuring the Sanquhar Declaration and for attending field conventicles. The sentence was drowning. They were tied to stakes in the Bladnoch estuary, the elder further out so that the younger might watch her die and recant; when the water reached the girl she was asked what she saw, and answered that she saw Christ suffering in one of His members. The local record of the executions is complete enough that attempts to argue the women were reprieved have not stood. Rev 2:10 is the text on the monument that stands there still. Mat 10:28 is the reason two women could not be moved by a rising tide. The dictionary records their names because Scripture records such names, and because a confession that cannot be held by an eighteen-year-old girl in cold water is not the confession these women held.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith; and constancy, as firmness of mind; stability in sentiments or affections.
webster_full: M'ARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the Christian faith, or by reason of his adherence to it.
CON'STANCY, n. Fixedness; a standing firm; firmness of mind; stability in sentiments, affections or purposes.
ABJURA'TION, n. The act of abjuring; a renunciation upon oath.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.

Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
corruption_summary: Two women were drowned in a tidal estuary for attending sermons, and the younger was asked to watch the elder die first.
corruption_paragraphs: The detail of the staggered stakes is the thing to hold. The sentence was designed not merely to kill but to break, by putting the hardest possible pressure on the youngest and most frightened. Mat 10:28 is the exact verse for that design, distinguishing what the persecutor can reach from what he cannot. Gal 2:20 is the answer the girl in fact gave: the life she lived in the flesh she lived by the faith of the Son of God, who loved her and gave Himself for her.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. One live misuse deserves naming: the treatment of martyr stories as national folklore, admired for Scottish stubbornness rather than received as a testimony to Christ. Rev 12:11 does not credit the overcoming to the character of the overcomers. It credits the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, and only then mentions that they loved not their lives unto the death.
